articles.title: ‘Slavery is not a thing of the past’: UN supports call for reparations
articles.summary: Slavery is not just a thing of the past. Its effects continue to be felt in systemic inequality and racism. This was reiterated on Monday by the UN Committee against Racial Discrimination (CERD) as the world marks the International Day of People of African Descent.
articles.content:
The committee is calling on States to implement comprehensive restorative justice, combining compensation, restitution, rehabilitation and structural reforms.

The passage of time cannot serve as a pretext for States to refuse to recognise these historical injustices or to adopt “appropriate measures of restorative justice and accountability for these crimes”, according to the committee.

Comprising18 independent human rights experts elected for four-year terms, the committee’s main task is to examine the periodic reports submitted by member countries on the measures taken to combat racism and discrimination.

It also advocates for comprehensive and far-reaching remedial measures, both financial, non-financial and structural, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-recurrence.

National plans and deadlines

“The elimination of racial discrimination cannot be effective, complete or sustainable without a full commitment to review and redress the ongoing harms and consequences of the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised slavery,” the experts said in a statement.

To ensure the effectiveness of reparations, they advocate the implementation of national action plans with specific deadlines, developed in consultation with people of African descent and the committees in charge of reparations.

The committee also called on States to repeal or revise laws and policies that perpetuate racism or discrimination or that obstruct restorative justice. It demanded transformations of laws, policies, and institutions that continue to perpetuate racial inequalities.

“Acknowledgments and apologies should be accompanied by concrete measures and should not replace other appropriate forms of redress,” the experts argued.

Private actors face responsibilities

CERD also examined the responsibility of private and other non-State actors, including religious organizations, universities, businesses, banks, insurers and other financial institutions that participated in, facilitated or profited from the trafficking of enslaved Africans.

The committee also called on States to ensure that these actors contribute effectively to restorative justice, in particular by recognising their historical role, opening relevant archives and contributing to reparation measures “in a manner proportionate to their involvement and the benefits they have derived from it”.

The committee stressed that these responsibilities remain relevant: the harms linked to the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised slavery persist in the form of “systemic racial discrimination and structural inequalities”.

Committee members specifically pointed to racialised violence, stereotypes and structural barriers that fuel disparities in education, health, economic mobility and environmental security.

These legacies of slavery have been “reinforced by policies perpetuating anti-Black racism”.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a major human rights initiative with potential for measurable positive change.
articles.personality_title: UN committee urges reparations to address lasting effects of slavery
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Slavery ended many years ago, but its effects still affect people today through unfair treatment and racism. On the International Day of People of African Descent, the United Nations Committee against Racial Discrimination (CERD) spoke about these ongoing problems.

**What happened** – The CERD, a group of 18 human rights experts, asked countries to take strong actions to fix the harm caused by slavery. They want governments to give compensation, change unfair laws, and work with people affected by slavery to create clear plans with deadlines. The committee also said private groups like banks and businesses that benefited from slavery should help with these efforts.

**Impact** – This is important because it recognizes that slavery’s effects are still alive in things like racism, violence, and unequal chances in school, health, and jobs. The committee’s call for real actions—not just apologies—means governments and companies must take responsibility and make changes that can help reduce these problems.

**What's next step** – Countries will need to create national plans to repair the damage caused by slavery. They will also have to review and change any laws that keep racism alive. Private organizations will be asked to be part of the solution by sharing information and contributing to reparations.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN committee is pushing for real and clear actions from governments and organizations to repair the lasting damage caused by slavery and ongoing racial discrimination.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le comité de l’ONU appelle à des réparations pour les effets durables de l’esclavage

articles.title: ‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
articles.summary: He was born without arms, a legacy of four decades of nuclear explosions at the Semipalatinsk test site in his native Kazakhstan.
articles.content:
Artist and anti-nuclear activist Karipbek Kuyukov walked through the halls of UN Headquarters in New York on Monday alongside diplomats, scientists and survivors, carrying a message he has spent his life delivering: no one should ever again suffer what his generation endured.

Mr. Kuyukov, who paints holding the brush with his lips and toes, was among the participants of a symbolic walk ahead of the General Assembly’s high-level meeting on the occasion of the International Day against Nuclear Tests, marked annually on 29 August.

The short procession, part of the #StepUp4Disarmament campaign, ended in front of a large photograph on display in the General Assembly building, depicting people demanding the closure of the Semipalatinsk site.

“I would like to tell our story, the story of Kazakhstan,” Mr. Kuyukov told UN News.

456 nuclear tests

Between 1949 and 1989, the Semipalatinsk site saw 456 nuclear tests. Hundreds of thousands of people living nearby were exposed to elevated levels of radiation, with consequences carried within families across generations.

“My parents were living witnesses of those tests, and as a result, I was born without arms,” Mr. Kuyukov said.

He was 20 years old when Kazakh poet Olzhas Suleimenov launched the Nevada-Semipalatinsk anti-nuclear movement.

© CTBTO/US Government

‘Entire nation rose up’

“The entire nation rose up against this monster, against the Semipalatinsk polygon,” he recalled.

The movement reached far beyond Kazakhstan.

Mr. Kuyukov remembered standing at a protest alongside a chief of the Shoshone people, whose lands lay near the United States test site in Nevada, and joining peaceful rallies at the gates of Semipalatinsk with activists from French Polynesia, where France conducted tests at Mururoa Atoll, and from Japan.

Shuttered for good

On 29 August 1991, the Semipalatinsk site was shut down, a date the General Assembly later proclaimed, at Kazakhstan’s initiative, as the International Day against Nuclear Tests. This year marks 35 years since the closure.

“I can say with pride that my country, Kazakhstan, began its path to sovereignty precisely with that peaceful decision,” Mr. Kuyukov said. “I believe this is a great honour for us and can serve as a worthy example for other countries.”

Every step counts

Addressing participants of the walk, UN High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu said the silence that fell upon Semipalatinsk 35 years ago “did not happen by chance”.

“It was achieved through the determination of people, communities and leaders who rejected nuclear testing,” she said.

Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov described the walk as “a very simple but very powerful way to remind us that every step towards disarmament matters”.

This year also marks the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the CTBT Organization, told the young people taking part in the walk that disarmament is “a journey that works across generations”.

“The day will come when your generation will lead, will make the decisions, will be in the boardrooms, will be in the assembly halls,” he said. “And we will be cheering on your great steps forward.”

UN News/Kulpash Konyrova

No one immune

Speaking later in the General Assembly, Ms. Nakamitsu warned that concerns about a possible resumption of nuclear explosive testing have re-emerged amid deep geopolitical tension.

She recalled the Secretary-General’s message: “the world must never witness another nuclear explosion.”

The President of the General Assembly, Annalena Baerbock, stressed that the consequences of nuclear explosions know no borders.

“In an interconnected world such as ours, there is no truly ‘remote region’ immune from the effects or dangers of nuclear testing,” she said.

Five generations of cancer

Among the speakers was Tina Cordova, a fourth-generation survivor of the 1945 Trinity test in New Mexico, who also joined the morning’s symbolic walk.

“We were the first people exposed to radiation anyplace in the world as ash fell from the sky in the days after the bomb,” she told the Assembly, describing five generations of cancer in her family. “We were never warned before or after of the danger, so we lived our lives off the land as we always did.”

She closed with an appeal to the delegates, saying that “after 81 years, it is time we set our families, our children and grandchildren free from nuclear threat.”

Message to the young

For Mr. Kuyukov, the fight is now about those who come next. Seeing young people join movements against nuclear weapons always reminds him that “in war, it is innocent children who suffer first.”

“The future is in their hands,” he said. “They, too, must secure a safe world for the next generation. We have experience and we can share it because we know how this is done.”

Asked what he would say to world leaders at a time when, in his words, the situation in the world has become dangerously tense, the artist called for reconciliation.

“To reach a new world – one of kindness, mercy and compassion – we need to let go of old grievances and past mistakes and leave them in history,” he stressed. “Now, we can only move forward together, showing the way to the new generation.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: What counts as real music? Australia’s charts just drew a line.
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For 16 weeks, an AI-generated variation of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” sat in Australia’s top 20 singles chart. At its peak, it hit number two. Listeners streamed it, and the chart counted it. And then the Australian Record Industry Association (ARIA) decided that probably shouldn’t keep happening. Starting today, […]
The post What counts as real music? Australia’s charts just drew a line. first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

For 16 weeks, an AI-generated variation of Madonna’s “Like a Prayer” sat in Australia’s top 20 singles chart. At its peak, it hit number two. Listeners streamed it, and the chart counted it. And then the Australian Record Industry Association (ARIA) decided that probably shouldn’t keep happening.

Starting today, wholly AI-generated tracks will be barred from the ARIA charts and from eligibility for the ARIA awards. Music where humans wrote the song and performed the lead vocal and primary instruments can still qualify. Fully machine-generated output is out.

“The ARIA Charts will always remain a transparent measurement of the music Australia consumes,” said ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd, “but a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent.”

Where the line falls

So, wholly AI-generated is out. AI-assisted, where the human is still driving creative decisions, stays in.

Sydney Conservatorium of Music composer and lecturer Alexis Weaver put it this way: “It can be quite hard to avoid AI tools in the current landscape. There is a way to use it while you’re still steering the ship and making the main creative choices.” That’s more or less what ARIA is trying to capture in rules: not whether AI touched the track, but whether a human was still at the wheel for the decisions that shaped it.

The new rules also require that eligible music come from legal AI services, not tools trained on artists’ work without permission. Music had been showing up on streaming platforms apparently built with unlicensed training data, a problem the chart rules now address alongside the creative question.

Australia isn’t doing this alone

ARIA’s move came alongside guidelines published in July by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry, the London-based body representing the global recording industry. Their standard: a chart-eligible track must be “substantially human made.”

The shared pressure behind both is straightforward. Generative AI has gotten good enough that listeners may not notice, or particularly care, whether a track was made by a person or a machine. Charts weren’t built for that. The practical question for the industry is when to draw the line, and the answer both bodies landed on is: now, while the distinction is still legible.

The question the charts can’t answer

Weaver described the debate around AI in music as “exceptionally fraught and very emotional for a lot of musicians.” That’s understating it. AI tools trained on existing recordings can now replicate styles, voices, and production techniques that took artists years to develop. Nobody has a tidy answer yet for what that means for the people whose work fed those models.

The Madonna cover’s 16 weeks in the top 20 is the uncomfortable data point nobody quite knows what to do with. Listeners didn’t reject it. It wasn’t exposed and abandoned when people found out. It just charted, week after week, because it sounded like something people wanted to hear. The chart ban settles what counts as eligible. What people choose to stream is another matter, and the industry has considerably less say in that.

Weaver called the ARIA move “a wonderful step forward” and said it sent a message about valuing human creativity. Whether the people doing the streaming see it the same way is a genuinely open question.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

The article provides detailed context about the policy, its rationale, and its alignment with global standards, making it a substantive and meaningful development.
articles.personality_title: Australia sets new rules to keep AI music off official charts

articles.title: Nigeria’s Dambe is evolving. Its communities should not be left behind
articles.summary: If decisions about the future of Dambe are made without meaningful participation from its communities, there is a risk that the sport's cultural context becomes secondary to its commercial value.
articles.content:
By Nshua Cali-Dibang

As Dambe fighters gather for a contest, the scene can look like a simple fight. Two opponents face one another, surrounded by drums, chants and spectators waiting for the first strike. Yet behind the spectacle is a tradition deeply associated with the Hausa people of Nigeria and West Africa.

Dambe is a traditional combat sport historically practised by Hausa communities, particularly among butchers and tradesmen. According to BBC Sport, the sport was associated with festivals and harvest periods and was regarded as a test of bravery. Its history has also been connected to preparing men for warfare and, in some communities, rites of passage.

Dambe is going global

For generations, therefore, Dambe has existed within particular communities and social relationships. But today, the sport is moving beyond those traditional settings. Its appearance on social media has introduced it to audiences far beyond Nigeria. Dambe Warriors, for example, used YouTube to transform local competitions into content for a global audience, with millions of views coming from outside Nigeria.

This visibility presents an important opportunity. Greater exposure can create new audiences, income and recognition for fighters. BBC Sport reported that Dambe's online popularity had grown dramatically, while promoters hoped the sport could move beyond its local origins and become internationally recognised.

But visibility also raises a question about who gets to define Dambe as it enters the mainstream.

Connected beliefs and traditions

One of the clearest examples is the spiritual dimension surrounding some Dambe fighters. Reporting by Al Jazeera documented fighters wearing amulets, undertaking fortification rituals and using herbal preparations before competitions. These practices demonstrate that, for some practitioners, Dambe is connected to beliefs and traditions that extend beyond the physical contest.

This raises an important question about how Indigenous cultural practices are interpreted. An object that may appear to an outside observer as decoration can carry a completely different meaning for the person who wears it. Rather than deciding what these practices mean from outside, their meaning should be understood through the voices of the people and communities who practise them.

Influence of professional sporting structures

Dambe is also changing structurally. Modern organisers are introducing rules intended to make competitions safer and easier to follow. According to BBC Sport, African Warriors introduced three three-minute rounds, a points system, and clearer definitions of knockdowns as part of efforts to make the sport safer and fairer.

These changes are not necessarily a threat to tradition. Professionalisation can bring better opportunities, safety measures, sponsorship and income for fighters. The same BBC report documented fighters earning prize money and organisers attracting international interest.

Yet modernisation raises another question: what should be preserved, and who decides?

The question of preservation

If Dambe becomes increasingly commercialised, who establishes the policies governing it? Should decisions come primarily from government and sports administrators, private promoters, cultural institutions, traditional authorities, or the communities that have historically practised the sport?

There may not be a simple answer. Regulation can provide structure and safety, while professionalisation can create opportunities that traditional competitions may not have been able to offer. But if decisions about the future of Dambe are made without meaningful participation from its communities, there is a risk that the sport's cultural context becomes secondary to its commercial value.

This is where Dambe becomes relevant to Indigenous rights.

Dambe’s future

Cultural heritage is not simply something to be displayed during festivals or packaged for outside audiences. It can be living knowledge, practised by communities and adapted by each generation. The question is therefore not whether Dambe should remain exactly as it was in the past. Communities themselves may want the sport to change.

The more important question is whether they have a meaningful voice in deciding how it changes.

As Dambe moves from community arenas to YouTube channels, organised championships and professional sporting structures, its future should involve the people who have carried the tradition forward. Fighters, elders, organisers, cultural practitioners and community members should be part of conversations about its regulation, representation, commercialisation and preservation.

The future of Dambe does not have to be a choice between tradition and modernity. The sport can grow while remaining connected to its cultural roots.

But growth should not mean that the communities that gave Dambe its meaning become spectators in the story of its future.

The question is no longer simply how far Dambe can go. It is who gets to decide where it goes.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the evolving traditional sport Dambe gaining global recognition while emphasizing the importance of Indigenous communities' meaningful participation in decisions about its future. This reflects a positive real-world impact on cultural preservation and Indigenous rights, with broad significance for cultural heritage and community empowerment.
articles.personality_title: Nigeria’s traditional sport Dambe gains global attention as communities seek a voice
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Dambe is a traditional combat sport from Nigeria, especially among the Hausa people. It has long been linked to festivals, bravery tests, and cultural rituals in local communities.

**What happened** – Dambe is becoming popular worldwide through social media platforms like YouTube, where videos of matches attract millions of viewers outside Nigeria. At the same time, modern rules and safety measures are being introduced to make the sport more professional.

**Impact** – This growing popularity offers new chances for fighters to earn money and gain recognition. However, it also raises important questions about who decides how Dambe should change—whether traditional communities, promoters, or officials. The spiritual and cultural meanings behind Dambe might be lost if local voices are not included.

**What's next step** – The future of Dambe depends on including the communities who have preserved it for generations in decisions about its rules, safety, and representation. This will help balance modern growth with respect for cultural traditions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – As Dambe reaches the world stage, its traditional communities must play a key role in shaping its future to keep the sport connected to its roots.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le sport traditionnel nigérian Dambe gagne en visibilité mondiale tandis que les communautés réclament leur voix
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Dambe est un sport de combat traditionnel du Nigeria, particulièrement pratiqué par le peuple Hausa. Il est lié depuis longtemps à des festivals, des épreuves de courage et des rituels culturels dans les communautés locales.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le Dambe devient populaire dans le monde entier grâce aux réseaux sociaux comme YouTube, où les vidéos des combats attirent des millions de spectateurs hors du Nigeria. En même temps, des règles modernes et des mesures de sécurité sont mises en place pour professionnaliser le sport.

**Impact** – Cette popularité croissante offre de nouvelles opportunités aux combattants pour gagner de l’argent et être reconnus. Mais cela soulève aussi la question de savoir qui décide de l’évolution du Dambe – les communautés traditionnelles, les promoteurs ou les autorités. Les significations spirituelles et culturelles risquent d’être perdues si les voix locales ne sont pas entendues.

**Prochaine étape** – L’avenir du Dambe dépend de l’inclusion des communautés qui l’ont préservé pendant des générations dans les décisions concernant ses règles, sa sécurité et sa représentation. Cela aidera à équilibrer la croissance moderne avec le respect des traditions culturelles.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Alors que le Dambe s’internationalise, ses communautés traditionnelles doivent jouer un rôle clé pour préserver le lien entre le sport et ses racines.
articles.personality_title_es: El deporte tradicional nigeriano Dambe gana atención global mientras las comunidades buscan tener voz
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Dambe es un deporte de combate tradicional de Nigeria, especialmente entre el pueblo Hausa. Ha estado ligado durante mucho tiempo a festivales, pruebas de valentía y rituales culturales en las comunidades locales.

**Qué pasó** – El Dambe se está haciendo popular en todo el mundo a través de redes sociales como YouTube, donde los videos de las peleas atraen millones de espectadores fuera de Nigeria. Al mismo tiempo, se están introduciendo reglas modernas y medidas de seguridad para profesionalizar el deporte.

**Impacto** – Esta creciente popularidad ofrece nuevas oportunidades para que los luchadores ganen dinero y reconocimiento. Sin embargo, también plantea preguntas sobre quién decide cómo debe cambiar el Dambe: las comunidades tradicionales, los promotores o las autoridades. Los significados espirituales y culturales podrían perderse si no se incluye la voz local.

**Próximo paso** – El futuro del Dambe depende de incluir a las comunidades que lo han conservado durante generaciones en las decisiones sobre reglas, seguridad y representación. Esto ayudará a equilibrar el crecimiento moderno con el respeto por las tradiciones culturales.

**Resumen en una frase** – A medida que el Dambe llega al escenario mundial, sus comunidades tradicionales deben tener un papel clave para mantener el deporte conectado con sus raíces.
